(I). WHETHER THE IMPUGNED NOTICE DATED 31.03.2015 REOPENING OF
ASSESSMENTS OF THE APPELLANTS FOR THE AY 2008-09 AND AY 2009-
10 SATISFIES THE ANVIL OF "REASON TO BELIEVE" UNDER SECTIONS 147-

SLP(C) No. 20045 of 2019 & Connected Matters Page 2 of 53
1. Leave granted.
2. These connected appeals arise from the self same judgment and
order dated 06.08.2019 passed by the High Court of Delhi in Writ
Petition (C) No. 10898 of 2015 preferred by the appellant herein, by
which the High Court dismissed the said writ petition and thereby
upheld the reassessment proceedings initiated by the respondent-revenue under Sections 147 and 148 of the Income Tax Act, 1961
respectively (hereinafter referred to as "the Act") in the case of the
appellants for AY 2008-09 and AY 2009-10, respectively.
A. FACTUAL MATRIX
3. Mr. Chetan Sabharwal, the appellant-assessee herein, along with
his brother - Mr. Nitin Sabharwal, the appellant-assessee in the
connected matters, and two other shareholders, entered into two
Share Purchase Agreements dated 19.10.2007 ("SPA") with GYS
Real Estate Pvt. Ltd/ ("Buyer Company") for sale of 7.5 Lakh equity
shares of one Pawan Impex (P.) Ltd. ("Company No. 1") and of 2.5
Lakh equity shares of another SVIIT Software (P.) Ltd. ("Company
No. 2") held by each of the parties for a total sale consideration of
Rs. 195 Crore and Rs. 60 Crore, respectively. The appellant and
other selling shareholders were each entitled to 1/4th share of this
total consideration. With respect to the company nos. 1 and 2, an
amount of Rs. 110 Crore and Rs. 22.5 Crore, respectively, was
received as advance during FY 2007-08/AY 2008-09 out of the sale
consideration of Rs. 195 Crore and Rs. 60 Crore, respectively. The
appellant's 1/4th share in this advance consideration amounted to
Rs. 27.5 Crore and 5.62 Crore, respectively. Further, the buyer
company made an additional payment of Rs. 18 Crore with respect
to the sale of the company no. 2's share. The appellant's 1/4th share

SLP(C) No. 20045 of 2019 & Connected Matters Page 3 of 53
in this additional payment amounted to Rs. 4.5 Crore. Therefore,
the total of the 1/4th share of the appellant in advance
consideration and additional payment aggregated to an amount of
Rs. 37.64 Crore.
4. On 25.09.2008, the appellant filed his ITR for AY 2008-09,
declaring a loss of Rs. 90.37 Lakh, which was accompanied by the
computation of total income along with the tax audit report. In the
return in Form ITR 4, particulars of the tax audit report obtained
had been filed, and therein a sum of Rs. 37.64 Crore has been
shown under the head sundry credit, which included the amount
of liability in the name of the buyer company aggregating to a tune
of Rs. 37.62 Crore.
5. As per the terms embodied in Article 1 read with Article 4 of the
SPA, the 'Closing' of sale of equity shares of company nos. 1 and 2
respectively in favour of the buyer company had to take place
subject to fulfilment of the conditions as stated in Article 4. At the
time of Closing, the total consideration of Rs. 195 Crore payable for
the shares of company no. 1 was reduced by Rs. 63.79 Crore, being
the amount of unsecured loan standing in the books of the
company, and by Rs. 3 Crore, being the estimated cost of
construction of building as per the SPA, and the buyer company
accordingly paid a net sale consideration of Rs. 128,20,66,501, of
which the appellant's 1/4th share was Rs. 32,05,16,625. Similarly,
with respect to company no. 2, the total consideration of Rs. 60
Crore was reduced by Rs. 18.99 Crore, being the amount of
unsecured loan standing in the books of the company, and by Rs.
60 Lakh, being the estimated cost of construction of building as per
the SPA, and the buyer company accordingly paid a net sale

SLP(C) No. 20045 of 2019 & Connected Matters Page 4 of 53
consideration of Rs. 40,40,84,770, of which the appellant's 1/4th
share was Rs. 10,10,21,192.
6. On 17.11.2008, the shares of company no. 1 were dematerialised
upon the request of the buyer company dated 19.11.2008, and
were transferred to Religare Securities Ltd. (Depositary under
NSDL), an associate company/concern of the Religare Group. On
25.09.2009, the appellant deposited amounts of Rs. 28 Crore and
Rs. 3.915 Crore, respectively, in the Capital Gain Savings Bank
Account No. 307802090000006 with the Union Bank of India, in
accordance with Section 54F(4) of the Act.
7. On 21.04.2010, the two appellants jointly purchased an undivided
and undefined 1/2 share in a residential property located in Delhi
for an aggregate consideration of Rs. 61 Crore. The said property
was purchased out of the capital gains arising in the hands of the
appellant and his brother from the sale of shares of company no. 1
and company no. 2, respectively, within a period of 2 years, thereby
entitling the appellant to the benefit of Section 54F of the Act.
8. On 06.08.2010, the respondent issued a notice under Section
142(1) of the Act, seeking an explanation on the nature of the
transaction with the buyer company amounting to Rs. 37.62 Crore,
and the production of the return documents of the buyer company
for the last 5 years, among other details. In response to the queries
raised by the respondent, the appellant submitted the requisite
details along with supporting documents on 05.10.2010.
9. Thereafter, on 13.12.2010, the respondent issued notices under
Section 133(6) of the Act to company no. 1, company no. 2 and the
buyer company, calling for information in relation to the
aforementioned transaction of sale of shares by the appellant. On

SLP(C) No. 20045 of 2019 & Connected Matters Page 5 of 53
16.12.2010, the company no. 1 and company no. 2 filed their reply
to the said notice, submitting the documents sought thereunder.
Similarly, on 16.12.2010, the buyer company filed its reply to the
said notice, submitting the documents sought.
10. On 22.12.2010, the assessment under Section 143(3) of the Act was
framed for AY 2008-09, whereby the returned income of the
appellant was accepted.
11. Subsequent to the completion of the assessment, the Investigation
Unit, Noida, under the DGIT (Inv.), Lucknow, conducted enquiries
into the value of the shares of company no. 1 and company no. 2
and prepared a report ("Investigation Report"). The report
concluded, prima facie, that the shares were overvalued when
compared with the cost of their land and building, which was much
lower than the transaction amounts of Rs. 195 Crore and Rs. 60
Crore, respectively. The enquiries also revealed that the appellants
purchased one-half share of property at Sikandara Road, New Delhi
in April 2010 through a court auction, and that the major source
of this investment was the sale proceeds of the shares of company
no. 1 and company no. 2.
12. Thereafter, on perusal of the investigation report and after a gap of
4 years, the respondent issued a notice dated 31.03.2015 under
Section 148 of the Act ("Impugned Notice") for reassessment in the
case of the appellant for AY 2008-09, calling upon the appellant to
file his return of income. By letter dated 24.04.2015, the
respondent communicated the recorded reasons under Section 148
of the Act for reopening the case of the appellant. On 20.05.2015,
the appellant filed legal objections to the initiation of the impugned
reassessment proceedings for AY 2008-09.

SLP(C) No. 20045 of 2019 & Connected Matters Page 6 of 53
13. On 24.09.2015, the respondent passed an order rejecting the legal
objections of the appellant for AY 2008-09. Aggrieved by the said
rejection of the legal objections against the initiation of
reassessment proceedings for AY 2008-09, the appellant filed a writ
petition bearing W.P.(C) No. 10898 of 2015 before the High Court.
The High Court, by the impugned judgment and order, dismissed
the writ petition filed by the appellant, thereby upholding the
initiation of reassessment proceedings by the respondent under
Section 147 of the Act in the case of the appellant for AY 2008-09.
14. In such circumstances referred to above, the appellant is here
before us with the present appeal.
B. SUBMISSIONS ON BEHALF OF THE APPELLANTS
15. Mr. Mukul Rohatgi, the learned senior counsel appearing for the
appellant, submitted that, after the expiry of 4 years from the end
of the relevant AYs, the respondent issued impugned notice dated
31.03.2015 under Section 148 of the Act, initiating reassessment
proceedings in the case of the appellant and his brother for AY
2008-09 and AY 2009-10, and that identical reasons to believe were
recorded by the respondent under Section 148(2) of the Act in the
case of both of them for both the years. He further submitted that
it is trite law that the initiation of reassessment proceedings under
Sections 147 and 148 of the Act, respectively, is required to be
tested on the reasons to believe as they stand recorded by the
respondent.
16. The learned senior counsel argued that there is an absence of valid
"reasons to believe" demonstrating escapement of income in the
present case. He submitted that, on a bare perusal of the reasons

SLP(C) No. 20045 of 2019 & Connected Matters Page 7 of 53
recorded for the said notice, the reasons recorded by the
respondent for alleging escapement of income in the hands of the
appellant and his brother are legally unsustainable inasmuch as:
(a) The sole basis for reopening is the alleged overvaluation of
shares sold by the appellant, which cannot result in
escapement of income in the hands of the seller, and no doubt
ever came to be raised on the genuineness of the sale, thereby
showing non-application of mind to the jurisdictional condition
of escapement of income;
(b) For AY 2008-09, there can be no escapement of income on the
sale of shares of company no. 1 and company no. 2, as the
transfer was complete only in AY 2009-10, upon fulfilment of
the conditions under Article 4 of the SPAs and delivery of share
certificates with transfer deed and/or transfer through Demat
Account;
(c) For AY 2009-10, the Long Term Capital Gains ("LTCG") on the
transfer was duly disclosed and offered to tax in the ITRs filed
by the appellant and his brother;
(d) The transaction was independently enquired into by the
respondent and confirmed by the said companies and the
buyer company in the scrutiny assessment under Section
143(3) of the Act for both AYs. The reassessment of the buyer
company on the same transaction also ended in acceptance of
its returned income;
(e) The alleged colourable deferment of LTCG and the resultant
claim under Section 54F, raised in the order disposing of the
objections, formed no part of the reasons recorded, and
amount to an improvement upon the same.

SLP(C) No. 20045 of 2019 & Connected Matters Page 8 of 53
17. The learned senior counsel further submitted that, in terms of the
Proviso 1 to Section 147 of the Act, reassessment beyond 4 years
from the end of the relevant AY, where an assessment has been
completed under Section 143(3), is permissible only if income has
escaped assessment by reason of the failure of the assessee to
disclose fully and truly all material facts necessary for assessment,
and that in the absence of such failure during the earlier scrutiny
proceedings, reassessment initiated after the said period is illegal.
Reliance was placed on various decisions to fortify the submission
that the respondent must come into possession of some fresh
tangible information relating to a concluded assessment which
exposes the falsity of the statement made by the assessee at the
time of the original assessment.
18. It was submitted that, in the case of the appellant, the transaction
of sale of shares of company no. 1 and company no. 2, respectively,
to the buyer company was fully disclosed in the accounts and the
ITRs, and was thoroughly examined, and that all information and
evidence was duly furnished for AY 2008-09 and AY 2009-10
respectively. He pointed out that at no stage has any failure on the
part of the appellant to disclose the primary facts been alleged or
made out. In this background, it was argued that since such failure
to disclose is a jurisdictional precondition under the Proviso 1 to
Section 147 of the Act, its absence renders the reassessment
initiated beyond 4 years from the end of the relevant AY without
jurisdiction.
19. The learned senior counsel further submitted that the
reassessment could be said to have been initiated on a mere change
of opinion, without any allegation, let alone evidence, of a failure on
the part of the appellant to disclose the primary facts. It was

SLP(C) No. 20045 of 2019 & Connected Matters Page 9 of 53
submitted that, in the case of the appellant, the record clearly
demonstrates that the transaction of sale of shares of company no.
1 and company no. 2 to the buyer company was specifically and
thoroughly examined, and that it was only thereafter that the
respondent found merit in the explanation offered by the appellant
and accepted the returned income without drawing any adverse
inference. He submitted that the mere fact that such opinion
formed by the respondent in favour of the appellant did not find
specific mention in the body of the assessment order does not, in
any way, dilute the formation of the opinion itself.
C. SUBMISSIONS ON BEHALF OF THE RESPONDENT
20. Ms. Nisha Bagchi, the learned senior counsel, along with Mr. K.M.
Nataraj, the learned ASG, appearing for the respondent-revenue,
submitted that the investigation report, which was made available
to the respondent by the Investigation Unit, Noida, subsequent to
the completion of the assessments, pointed out the overvaluation
of the shares and constituted specific, reliable and tangible
information sufficient to form a reason to believe that income had
escaped assessment. The said investigation report concludes as
follows:
"It can be prima facie concluded that the value of shares are
overvalued to the extent of ₹109,80,00,000/- (In the case of
M/S Pawan Impex Limited) and ₹40,40,28,000/- (in the
case of SVIIT Software Private Limited) going by the cost of
land and Building, which is much lower than the
transaction amount of ₹195,00,00,000/- in the case of M/S
Pawan Impex Private Limited plus ₹60,00,00,000/- in the
case of SVIIT Software Private Limited"
21. It was further submitted on behalf of the respondent-revenue that
as per the settled law, whether the facts stated in the letter are true

SLP(C) No. 20045 of 2019 & Connected Matters Page 10 of 53
or not is not the concern at this stage, as the truth of the allegations
may be established after making the necessary enquiries, and that,
at the stage of issuance of the notice, the only question is whether
there was credible material on which a reasonable person could
have formed the requisite belief. On these parameters, it was
contended that the notices have been validly issued on a reason to
believe formed on the basis of tangible material, and that the
respondent has duly recorded reasons which have a live nexus to
the notice. After perusing the letter dated 15.10.2015, the other
correspondence in this regard and the report of the Investigation
Unit, the respondent believed that the shares had been overvalued,
that the capital gains were adjusted in future years and that
deductions were also claimed under Section 54F of the Act. The AO
had recorded that "with respect to the share transactions, the capital
gain earned, and deduction on the same claimed. I have the reasons
to believe that substantial amount has escaped assessment during
the assessment years 2008-09 and 2009-10".
22. In respect of the assessee - Mr. Chetan Sabharwal, the respondent-revenue submitted that the original assessment orders for both AYs
passed under Section 143(3) of the Act do not indicate that the
respondent formed any opinion on the issue on which reopening
has been ordered, and that the record indicates that the issue of
overvaluation of shares was not considered during the scrutiny
assessment. It was contended that, the order under Section 143(3)
of the Act being a non-speaking order, no opinion can be attributed
to the respondent on the issues sought to be raised in the proposed
reassessment proceedings. As regards the requirement under the
proviso to Section 147 of the Act that the under-assessment must
have occurred by reason of, inter alia, the failure of the assessee to
disclose fully and truly all material facts necessary for his

SLP(C) No. 20045 of 2019 & Connected Matters Page 11 of 53
assessment, it was submitted that the same essentially involves
questions of fact, which stand relegated to the adjudicating
authority. The Act postulates a duty on every assessee to disclose
fully and truly all material facts necessary for his assessment. It
was further submitted that the Assistant Commissioner of Income
Tax, while disposing of the objections against reassessment by his
order dated 24.09.2011, specifically recorded that the DDIT
(Investigation), Noida, had clearly mentioned that the mechanism
through which the net worth of the shares was calculated, and the
due diligence report of the shares, were not provided despite the
assessee being repeatedly asked to do so.
23. In respect of the assessee - Mr. Nitin Sabharwal, it was further
submitted on behalf of the respondent-revenue that only an
intimation under Section 143(1) of the Act was issued accepting his
returns, and that the notice was issued within the time prescribed
under Section 149(1)(b) of the Act on the basis of a valid reason to
believe. It was contended that the contentions relating to change of
opinion or failure to make full disclosure are not relevant to the
reassessment proceedings in his case. It was further submitted that
the only criteria for assessing income under Section 147 of the Act
are the existence of a valid reason recorded by the respondent and
the satisfaction of the jurisdictional Principal Commissioner, both
of which stand satisfied on the facts of the present assessment.
D. ISSUES FOR DETERMINATION
24. Having heard the learned counsel appearing for the parties and
having gone through the materials on record, the sole question that
falls for our consideration is whether the impugned notice dated
31.03.2015 seeking to reopen the assessments of the appellants for

SLP(C) No. 20045 of 2019 & Connected Matters Page 12 of 53
the AY 2008-09 and AY 2009-10, respectively, satisfies the anvil of
"reason to believe" under Section 147-148 of the Act and, thus, is
valid?
E. ANALYSIS
(I). Whether the impugned notice dated 31.03.2015 reopening of
assessments of the appellants for the AY 2008-09 and AY 2009-
10 satisfies the anvil of "reason to believe" under Section 147-
148 of the Act and, thus, is valid?
25. Before dealing with the rival submissions canvassed on either side,
a bare reading of Sections 147-148 of the Act, respectively, that
deal with reopening of the assessment must be undertaken.
26. Section 147 of the Act, as it stood on 31.03.2015, reads as follows:
"Section 147. Income escaping assessment.- If
the Assessing Officer, has reason to believe that any
income chargeable to tax has escaped assessment for any
assessment year, he may, subject to the provisions of
sections 148 to 153, assess or reassess such income and
also any other income chargeable to tax which has
escaped assessment and which comes to his notice
subsequently in the course of the proceedings under this
section, or recompute the loss or the depreciation allowance
or any other allowance, as the case may be, for the
assessment year concerned (hereafter in this section and in
sections 148 to 153 referred to as the relevant assessment
year):
Provided that where an assessment under sub-section
(3) of section 143 or this section has been made for the
relevant assessment year, no action shall be taken under
this section after the expiry of four years from the end of the
relevant assessment year, unless any income chargeable to
tax has escaped assessment for such assessment year by
reason of the failure on the part of the assessee to make a
return under section 139 or in response to a notice issued
under sub-section (1) of section 142 or section 148 or to

SLP(C) No. 20045 of 2019 & Connected Matters Page 13 of 53
disclose fully and truly all material facts necessary for his
assessment, for that assessment year:
Provided further that the Assessing Officer may
assess or reassess such income, other than the income
involving matters which are the subject matters of any
appeal, reference or revision, which is chargeable to tax and
has escaped assessment.
Explanation 1.-Production before the Assessing
Officer of account books or other evidence from which
material evidence could with due diligence have been
discovered by the Assessing Officer will not necessarily
amount to disclosure within the meaning of the foregoing
proviso.
Explanation 2.-For the purposes of this section, the
following shall also be deemed to be cases where income
chargeable to tax has escaped assessment, namely:
(a) where return of income has been furnished by the
assessee although his total income or the total income of
any other person in respect of which he is assessable under
this Act during the previous year exceeded the maximum
amount which is not chargeable to income-tax;
(b) where a return of income has been furnished by
the assessee but no assessment has been made and it is
noticed by the Assessing Officer that the assessee has
understated the income or has claimed excessive loss,
deduction, allowance or relief in the return;
(c) where an assessment has been made, but-
(i) income chargeable to tax has been
underassessed; or
(ii) such income has been assessed at too low a rate;
or
(iii) such income has been made the subject of
excessive relief under this Act; or
(iv) excessive loss or depreciation allowance or any
other allowance under this Act has been computed.
Explanation 3.-For the purpose of assessment or
reassessment under this section, the Assessing Officer may
assess or reassess the income in respect of any issue,
which has escaped assessment, and such issue comes to
his notice subsequently in the course of the proceedings
under this section, notwithstanding that the reasons for
such issue have not been included in the reasons recorded
under sub -section (2) of section 148."
(Emphasis Supplied)

SLP(C) No. 20045 of 2019 & Connected Matters Page 14 of 53
27. Section 148 of the Act, as it stood on 31.03.2015, reads as follows:
"Section 148. Issue of notice where income has
escaped assessment.- (1) Before making the assessment,
reassessment or recomputation under section 147, the
Assessing Officer shall serve on the assessee a notice
requiring him to furnish within such period, as may be
specified in the notice, a return of his income or the
income of any other person in respect of which he is
assessable under this Act during the previous year
corresponding to the relevant assessment year, in the
prescribed form and verified in the prescribed manner and
setting forth such other particulars as may be prescribed;
and the provisions of this Act shall, so far as may be, apply
accordingly as if such return were a return required to be
furnished under section 139:
Provided that in a case-
(a) where a return has been furnished during the
period commencing on the 1st day of October, 1991 and
ending on the 30th day of September, 2005 in response to a
notice served under this section, and
(b) subsequently a notice has been served under sub-section (2) of section 143 after the expiry of twelve months
specified in the proviso to sub-section (2) of section 143, as
it stood immediately before the amendment of said sub-section by the Finance Act, 2002 (20 of 2002) but before the
expiry of the time limit for making the assessment,
reassessment or recomputation as specified in sub-section
(2) of section 153, every such notice referred to in this clause
shall be deemed to be a valid notice:
Provided further that in a case-
(a) where a return has been furnished during the
period commencing on the 1st day of October, 1991 and
ending on the 30th day of September, 2005, in response to
a notice served under this section, and
(b) subsequently a notice has been served under
clause (ii) of sub-section (2) of section 143 after the expiry of
twelve months specified in the proviso to clause (ii) of sub-section (2) of section 143, but before the expiry of the time
limit for making the assessment, reassessment or
recomputation as specified in sub- section (2) of section 153,
every such notice referred to in this clause shall be deemed
to be a valid notice.

SLP(C) No. 20045 of 2019 & Connected Matters Page 15 of 53
Explanation.-For the removal of doubts, it is hereby
declared that nothing contained in the first proviso or the
second proviso shall apply to any return which has been
furnished on or after the 1st day of October, 2005 in
response to a notice served under this section.
(2) The Assessing Officer shall, before issuing any
notice under this section, record his reasons for doing so."
(Emphasis Supplied)
28. A conjoint reading of Sections 147 and 148 of the Act respectively
makes it clear that the power to reopen an assessment is not
unfettered and is hedged with conditions, the first being that the
AO must have reason to believe that income chargeable to tax has
escaped assessment, which is the jurisdictional foundation for
assuming the power to reassess. Once this threshold is met, the
AO is also empowered to bring to tax any other escaped income that
comes to his notice in the course of the reassessment proceedings,
provided the reason or at least one of the reasons, projected for
reopening is eventually found to be escaped income. However,
where the original assessment has been completed under Section
143(3) of the Act, a further safeguard is introduced by the proviso
to Section 147, whereby a notice beyond 4 years from the end of
the relevant AY can be sustained only if the escapement of income
is attributable to the failure of the assessee to disclose fully and
truly all material facts necessary for his assessment, and the
existence of such failure thus becomes a condition precedent to the
exercise of jurisdiction. Further, the power to reopen an
assessment is not confined to cases where the assessee has
concealed his income, and extends also to cases where, though
there has been no concealment, the respondent has reason to
believe, in consequence of tangible material in his possession, that
income has escaped assessment. Section 148 then operates as the
procedural safeguard, as it requires service of a notice on the

SLP(C) No. 20045 of 2019 & Connected Matters Page 16 of 53
assessee before the reassessment is undertaken, and, more
importantly, mandates that the AO record his reasons before
issuing the notice.
29. In the present case, the revenue's stand is that it issued the
impugned notice under Section 148 of the Act on the strength of
the investigation report submitted by the DGIT Investigation Unit,
Noida, which constituted specific and tangible material on the
overvaluation of shares. Thus, at the stage of issuing the notice, the
only question that would be relevant is whether there was any
credible material on which a reasonable person could form the
requisite belief, the truth of the allegations being a matter for
enquiry in the reassessment proceedings. The assessees' stand is
that the reasons recorded for the impugned notice proceed solely
on the alleged overvaluation of shares, which cannot result in
escapement of income in the hands of the sellers and raises no
doubt on the genuineness of the sale, and that the grounds of
colourable deferment of LTCG and the claim under Section 54F of
the Act, raised later in the order disposing of the objections, are an
improvement on the reasons recorded. Further, the transaction
having been examined in the scrutiny assessment under Section
143(3) of the Act, the reassessment amounts to a mere change of
opinion.
30. In order to determine whether the impugned notice satisfied the
test of "reason to believe" as required under section 147 of the Act,
we have to understand the meaning and scope of the said
expression.

SLP(C) No. 20045 of 2019 & Connected Matters Page 17 of 53
(a) Contours of the expression "reason to believe" under Sections
147 and 148 of the Act.
31. In the case of Calcutta Discount Co. Ltd. v. ITO, reported in
(1961) 41 ITR 191 (SC), the Constitution Bench of this Court
observed that the duty of the assessee is to disclose fully and truly
all primary relevant facts, and that it does not extend beyond this.
It was further observed that, if there were in fact some reasonable
grounds for thinking that there had been non-disclosure of any
primary fact having a material bearing on the question of under-assessment, that would be sufficient to give the AO jurisdiction to
issue the notice, and that the adequacy of such grounds is not open
to the court's investigation. It was held that all that is necessary is
that the AO had, when he assumed jurisdiction, some prima facie
grounds or reasons for thinking that there had been some non-disclosure of material facts, and that it is the duty of the assessee
who contends that jurisdiction was lacking to establish that the AO
had no material at all before him for believing that there had been
such non-disclosure. The relevant observations made by this Court
are as under:
"13. We have therefore come to the conclusion that while the
duty of the assessee is to disclose fully and truly all primary
relevant facts, it does not extend beyond this.
14. The position therefore is that if there were in fact some
reasonable grounds for thinking that there had been any
